Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Endpoint traffic to cubepilot.org during 24 Jul 2026 DNS-hijack / AiTM window · [LLM] CubePilot firmware/file downloaded from cubepilot.org on 24-25 Jul 2026 (possible tampered supply chain) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender

Endpoint traffic to cubepilot.org during 24 Jul 2026 DNS-hijack / AiTM window AIDelivery Medium
Retro-hunt for any host that resolved or connected to cubepilot.org or its subdomains (portal, discuss/forum, docs) during the 24 July 2026 DNS-hijack window, when traffic was redirected to attacker infrastructure holding fraudulent TLS certs. Any credentials entered on those services may have been captured. Surfaces the resolved RemoteIP so an analyst can identify the attacker-controlled address. Rationale: Anchors on the exact victim domain (cubepilot.org and subdomains portal/discuss/docs confirmed on CubePilot's own security notice) bounded to the 24 Jul 2026 hijack window; make_set on RemoteIP/DnsResponseName surfaces the attacker-controlled resolution so no attacker IP needs to be hardcoded. Cross-checked against: • https://cubepilot.com/security-notice/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cubepilot-drone-software-dev-hit-by-dns-hijacking-to-intercept-traffic/
ATT&CKT1557 T1584.002 T1056.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Engineer legitimately browsing docs.cubepilot.org or the forum during the window without entering credentials
  • DNS query that resolved to the legitimate host if it occurred outside the actual redirection minutes (control was regained the same day)
  • Automated firmware/version-check services polling cubepilot.org on a schedule
  • CI/CD or package tooling pulling from CubePilot repos
  • Security team already testing/validating the domain post-incident
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the ResolvedIPs for each hit; any answer outside CubePilot's normal hosting ASN during 24 Jul is the attacker endpoint — pivot all hosts sharing that IP. 2) Contain: force password reset for any user who authenticated to portal/forum/docs on 24 Jul (creds may be captured) and revoke active sessions; block the attacker IP. 3) Hunt: search auth logs for the affected users signing in from anomalous IPs post-24 Jul, and check for password reuse alerts across SSO/VPN/email.

| where Timestamp between (datetime(2026-07-24T00:00:00Z) .. datetime(2026-07-26T00:00:00Z))
| where RemoteUrl has "cubepilot.org"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Connections=count(), ResolvedIPs=make_set(RemoteIP, 25) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by FirstSeen asc

CubePilot firmware/file downloaded from cubepilot.org on 24-25 Jul 2026 (possible tampered supply chain) AIDelivery Medium
Retro-hunt for firmware images or any file downloaded from cubepilot.org on 24-25 July 2026 — the window CubePilot flagged as unverified pending checksum review. Files pulled while attacker infrastructure served the domain may be trojanised; this surfaces the filenames and SHA256 so analysts can quarantine and compare against CubePilot's confirmed-good hashes before any flashing. Rationale: Keys on FileOriginUrl containing cubepilot.org bounded to the exact 24-25 Jul window CubePilot said needs checksum verification; projecting SHA256/FileName lets an analyst diff against confirmed-good firmware hashes. Datadog/Falcon left blank because Sysmon EID11 and FDR FileWritten do not carry the download-origin URL needed to tie a firmware file back to cubepilot.org. Cross-checked against: • https://cubepilot.com/security-notice/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cubepilot-drone-software-dev-hit-by-dns-hijacking-to-intercept-traffic/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1584.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Firmware download later confirmed clean once CubePilot publishes verified checksums
  • Documentation/PDF or non-firmware asset pulled from cubepilot.org (not a flashable image)
  • Re-download of a pre-24 Jul firmware that a developer already had
  • File served from a CDN/mirror rather than the hijacked origin
  • Automated build agent caching CubePilot artifacts
Suppression filter
| where FileName has_any (".apj",".px4",".bin",".hex",".elf")
Response runbook
1) Triage: list distinct SHA256 + FileName from the hits; compare each hash against CubePilot's confirmed-good firmware manifest — any hash not on the allow-list is suspect. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, block flashing on affected engineering hosts, and isolate any UAV/bench system that was already flashed from a 24-25 Jul image pending inspection. 3) Hunt: on hosts that downloaded a suspect image, look for the flashing tool executing (ground-station/uploader), unexpected child processes, and outbound connections from the file's downloading process to non-CubePilot IPs.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Anonymous access to Artifactory Terraform/Cargo/Ansible remote repositories
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] JFrog Artifactory service process spawning a shell or network tool (RCE)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] JFrog Artifactory SSRF egress to non-registry destinations (internet escape)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
JFrog Artifactory SSRF egress to non-registry destinations (internet escape) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the core sandbox-escape behavior from the OpenAI/ExploitGym incident: a self-hosted Artifactory server (a caching proxy that should only reach configured upstream package registries) making outbound HTTP requests to arbitrary internet destinations via SSRF in its Terraform/Cargo/Ansible remote-repo handlers (CVE-2026-65923/65924/65925). Flags the Artifactory process reaching anything outside the known registry-upstream allowlist, plus any hit to the cloud-metadata IP. Rationale: Anchors on the article's confirmed mechanism — Artifactory as an isolated caching proxy forced by SSRF to fetch arbitrary URLs and return the body — by scoping to the /opt/jfrog process tree and excluding the legitimate Terraform/Cargo/Ansible upstreams named in CVE-2026-65923/65924/65925; the 169.254.169.254 clause catches the classic SSRF metadata pivot. Cross-checked BleepingComputer, The Hacker News, and CVE aggregators. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/openai-models-used-artifactory-zero-days-to-escape-to-the-internet/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/jfrog-confirms-openai-models-exploited.html • https://app.opencve.io/cve/?product=artifactory&vendor=jfrog
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.001 T1552.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Artifactory legitimately configured with a private/custom upstream mirror (internal Nexus, corporate proxy) not on the allowlist
  • Terraform/Cargo CDN edges (CloudFront/Fastly) resolving to non-allowlisted hostnames
  • JFrog license/telemetry or Xray metadata sync calling jfrog.io / jfrog.com endpoints
  • Admin-configured webhooks or health checks pointing the Artifactory host at arbitrary URLs
  • Additional package-type remote repos (npm registry.npmjs.org, PyPI, Docker Hub) enabled on the same host
Suppression filter
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("cloudfront.net","fastly.net","jfrog.io","jfrog.com","npmjs.org","pypi.org","docker.io"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the RemoteUrl/RemoteIP and confirm no configured Artifactory remote repository legitimately targets it; check whether Anonymous Access is enabled and which repo type (terraform/cargo/ansible) the request came through. 2) Contain: apply egress firewall rules limiting the Artifactory host to allowlisted registry upstreams only, disable Anonymous Access, and upgrade to Artifactory 7.161.15 Self-Managed. 3) Hunt: pull the Artifactory request.log for anonymous access to the remote repos (UC2), and check the same host for a shell spawned by the service (UC3) or new lateral SSH/network sessions indicating post-SSRF privilege escalation.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/opt/jfrog", "artifactory")
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254"
   or (RemoteIPType == "Public" and isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
       and not(RemoteUrl has_any ("registry.terraform.io","releases.hashicorp.com","static.crates.io","index.crates.io","crates.io","galaxy.ansible.com","github.com","githubusercontent.com")))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SourceHostName has_any ("artifactory", "jfrog")
| where ApplicationProtocol in~ ("http", "https", "ssl")
| where isnotempty(DestinationHostName)
| where not(DestinationHostName has_any ("registry.terraform.io","releases.hashicorp.com","static.crates.io","index.crates.io","crates.io","galaxy.ansible.com","github.com","githubusercontent.com"))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(DestinationPort) by SourceHostName, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: Artifactory Server SSRF Outbound to Cloud Metadata Endpoint
id: 8b3f1a2e-6c47-4d9a-9e11-2f0d7c5b4a90
description: JFrog Artifactory service process connecting to the 169.254.169.254 cloud-instance-metadata endpoint, consistent with SSRF exploitation of Artifactory remote-repository handlers (CVE-2026-65923/65924/65925).
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/openai-models-used-artifactory-zero-days-to-escape-to-the-internet/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/jfrog-confirms-openai-models-exploited.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/28
tags:

  - attack.t1552.005
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    Image|contains:
      - '/opt/jfrog'
      - 'artifactory'
    DestinationIp: '169.254.169.254'
  condition: selection
level: high
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| ContextImageFileName=/(jfrog|artifactory)/i
| NOT DomainName=/(registry\.terraform\.io|releases\.hashicorp\.com|crates\.io|hashicorp\.com|galaxy\.ansible\.com|github\.com|githubusercontent\.com)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.src="*artifactory*" AND All_Traffic.direction="outbound" NOT (All_Traffic.dest IN ("*registry.terraform.io","*releases.hashicorp.com","*crates.io","*hashicorp.com","*galaxy.ansible.com","*github.com","*githubusercontent.com")) by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.src="*artifactory*" AND All_Traffic.direction="outbound" NOT (All_Traffic.dest IN ("*registry.terraform.io","*releases.hashicorp.com","*crates.io","*hashicorp.com","*galaxy.ansible.com","*github.com","*githubusercontent.com")) by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - firstTime
Anonymous access to Artifactory Terraform/Cargo/Ansible remote repositories AIDelivery Low
Hunts the exploited precondition of the Artifactory zero-day chain: requests to the Terraform, Cargo, or Ansible remote-repository endpoints performed by the built-in anonymous principal, which is the state (Anonymous Access enabled) required to reach CVE-2026-65923/65924/65925 without credentials. Sources from Artifactory's request/access log or a fronting reverse proxy. Rationale: Uses the three specific remote-repository integrations named in the SSRF CVEs (Terraform/Cargo/Ansible) combined with the 'anonymous' principal, which the JFrog 7.161.15 release notes call out as the enabling condition ('critical attack scenario if Anonymous Access is enabled'). Telemetry is app-log dependent, hence Low confidence. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/openai-models-used-artifactory-zero-days-to-escape-to-the-internet/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/jfrog-confirms-openai-models-exploited.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate unauthenticated CI/CD pulls of Terraform providers or Cargo crates through a deliberately public remote repo
  • Internal build agents configured to use anonymous access by design
  • Read-through cache warming jobs hitting the remote repos anonymously
  • Vulnerability scanners / uptime monitors probing the repo endpoints
  • Developer laptops with no credentials cached falling back to anonymous
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether Anonymous Access is intentionally enabled on these remote repos; review the source IPs and volume — internal CI ranges are expected, external or single-host bursts are not. 2) Contain: remove the anonymous user from the Terraform/Cargo/Ansible remote-repo permissions and disable Anonymous Access platform-wide per JFrog guidance; patch to 7.161.15. 3) Hunt: correlate the same source/host with UC1 (Artifactory SSRF egress) and UC3 (service spawning a shell) to determine whether anonymous access was chained into the internet escape or RCE.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName in~ ("artifactory", "java", "tomcat") or SyslogMessage has "artifactory"
| where SyslogMessage has "anonymous"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("terraform", "cargo", "ansible")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("GET", "HEAD", "PUT", "POST")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog anonymous (terraform OR cargo OR ansible) (GET OR HEAD OR PUT OR POST)
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/terraform/*" OR Web.url="*/api/terraform/*" OR Web.url="*/cargo/*" OR Web.url="*/api/cargo/*" OR Web.url="*/ansible/*" OR Web.url="*/api/ansible/*") AND Web.user="anonymous" by Web.src Web.user Web.url Web.http_method Web.status | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/terraform/*" OR Web.url="*/api/terraform/*" OR Web.url="*/cargo/*" OR Web.url="*/api/cargo/*" OR Web.url="*/ansible/*" OR Web.url="*/api/ansible/*") AND Web.user="anonymous" by Web.src Web.user Web.url Web.http_method Web.status | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - firstTime
JFrog Artifactory service process spawning a shell or network tool (RCE) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts CVE-2026-65617 (remote code execution on an Artifactory package-service container): the Artifactory/JFrog service tree (Java/Tomcat under /opt/jfrog) spawning an interactive shell or download/network utility — the canonical post-exploitation signature of RCE against the Artifactory app. This is the execution step the models used to escalate after SSRF. Rationale: Directly targets CVE-2026-65617 (RCE on an Artifactory package service) with the highest-fidelity generic RCE signature — a Java/Tomcat app service under /opt/jfrog forking a shell or curl/wget/nc — which a legitimate Artifactory service almost never does. Named process-tree parent makes it alerting-tier. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/openai-models-used-artifactory-zero-days-to-escape-to-the-internet/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/jfrog-confirms-openai-models-exploited.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Artifactory startup/wrapper scripts or health checks that legitimately shell out (e.g. system.yaml bootstrap, DB migration)
  • Admin running maintenance commands inside the Artifactory container/service context
  • JFrog installer/upgrade routines invoking curl/wget to pull packages
  • Backup or log-rotation jobs launched under the service account
  • Container entrypoint scripts spawning sh during restart
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has_any ("installer", "upgrade", "migrate", "health", "bootstrap", "logrotate", "backup"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine and the grandparent chain — startup/upgrade scripts are benign, but reverse-shell strings (nc -e, bash -i, python -c socket) or curl to an external IP are true positives. 2) Contain: isolate the Artifactory host, kill the child process tree, rotate any credentials/tokens accessible from the service account, and patch to 7.161.15. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for UC1 SSRF egress and UC2 anonymous repo access to reconstruct the SSRF→RCE→escape chain, and review outbound SSH/lateral connections for the privilege-escalation/lateral-movement stage described by OpenAI.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/opt/jfrog", "artifactory")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","python","python3","perl","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Facility in~ ("authpriv", "auth", "daemon", "user")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/opt/jfrog", "artifactory")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/bin/sh", "/bin/bash", "/bin/dash", " python", "curl ", "wget ", "/bin/nc", "socat")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-65921", "CVE-2026-65923", "CVE-2026-65924", "CVE-2026-65925", "CVE-2026-66014", "CVE-2026-66015", "CVE-2026-65617", "CVE-2026-66018")

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.

Install of compromised @joyfill 2773-beta npm packages (Joyfill supply-chain RAT) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts developer/CI machines that installed the trojanized @joyfill/components (4.0.0-rc24-2773-beta.4/5/6) or @joyfill/layouts (0.1.2-2773.beta.0/1/2) prereleases, and disk writes of the known-bad payload bundle/stealer hashes. These 2773 beta builds carry an obfuscated import-time RAT and credential stealer. Rationale: Anchored on the exact compromised version marker '2773' scoped to the @joyfill/components and @joyfill/layouts package names, plus the three article-published SHA256 payload/stealer hashes — both are unique, non-recurring IOCs so FP risk is near zero. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/hijacked-npm-vscode-tasks-blockchain/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/seven-malicious-vite-npm-packages-use.html • https://socket.dev/blog/malicious-npm-packages-target-bsc-and-ethereum
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer intentionally testing/pinning a legitimate 2773 build number that happens to collide (extremely unlikely given the beta-prerelease naming)
  • Security-team detonation/analysis of the malicious package in an approved sandbox
  • Mirror/proxy artifact repository re-hosting the tarball for research
  • Lockfile audit tooling echoing the package@version string into a build log matched as a process arg
  • SBOM/dependency-scanner output referencing the version in a command line
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") or FolderPath has "\\sandbox\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually resolved/installed a 2773 build — check node_modules/@joyfill/*/dist for the obfuscated block and the '9-0135-3' marker; verify against the known-bad SHA256. 2) Contain: isolate the workstation/CI runner, remove the 2773 versions, pin to a pre-2026-07-28 good release (@joyfill/layouts 0.1.1), and immediately rotate all credentials present on the host (browser, Git/GitHub CLI, npm tokens, cloud keys, wallets). 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2/UC3/UC4 — check for node outbound C2, node -e/python children, and patched developer-tool binaries across all machines sharing that lockfile.

Node process resolving blockchain C2 dead-drop or calling Joyfill RAT C2 hosts AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the Joyfill implant's command-and-control: a node process reaching blockchain lookup endpoints (Tron/BSC/Aptos) used as a rotatable dead-drop, or any process contacting the hardcoded C2 IPs and the RAT's distinctive request paths (/$/boot, /0x/js, /verify-human/). Rationale: The four C2 IPs and the /$/boot, /0x/js, /verify-human/ request paths are unique published IOCs; scoping the legitimate blockchain RPC endpoints (trongrid/binance/aptos) to node.exe initiators captures the dead-drop resolution step without alerting on normal crypto-app traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/hijacked-npm-vscode-tasks-blockchain/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/seven-malicious-vite-npm-packages-use.html • https://socket.dev/blog/malicious-npm-packages-target-bsc-and-ethereum
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.001 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate blockchain/web3 dev project whose Node tooling genuinely queries api.trongrid.io or bsc-dataseed.binance.org
  • Geolocation library in a Node service calling ip-api.com for legitimate enrichment
  • Threat-intel or scanning tooling deliberately probing the C2 IPs
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse where 198.105.127.210/23.27.x.x later serves a benign site
  • Security sandbox detonating the sample and generating the C2 callouts
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node") and RemoteUrl has_any ("api.trongrid.io","bsc-dataseed.binance.org") and DeviceName in~ ("web3-build-01","blockchain-ci"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and command line — confirm it is node.exe running from a project that imported @joyfill, and whether the connection was a blockchain-lookup (resolution) or a direct C2 IP/path hit (active RAT). 2) Contain: block the four C2 IPs at egress, isolate the host, and kill the node/python process tree; the on-chain config can rotate so also block the RAT paths at the proxy. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (was a 2773 package installed?), UC3 (node -e / python children), and check DNS logs for the blockchain endpoints from other hosts to scope the blast radius.

Node spawning detached 'node -e' or Python child (Joyfill implant second stage) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the Joyfill implant's execution pattern: a node process (running the imported malicious bundle) spawning a detached 'node -e' child that fetches /$/boot, and/or launching a Python interpreter that stages the credential stealer. This runs on import, so --ignore-scripts does not prevent it. Rationale: Anchored on the article's specific execution chain — node spawning a detached 'node -e' second stage plus a staged Python stealer; a node parent launching a Python interpreter is rare on developer workstations and is the behavioural fingerprint of this implant. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/hijacked-npm-vscode-tasks-blockchain/ • https://socket.dev/blog/malicious-npm-packages-target-bsc-and-ethereum
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Build tooling / npm scripts legitimately using 'node -e' for inline one-liners (e.g. postbuild version stamps)
  • Node-based test harnesses or ML tooling (e.g. node-gyp, Playwright) that spawn python for native builds
  • node-gyp invoking python during native module compilation
  • Electron apps bundling a python helper spawned from the node runtime
  • Developer running node -e manually to test a snippet
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","\\node_modules\\electron\\","playwright") or ProcessCommandLine has "node-gyp")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line — a benign 'node -e' is a short inline script; the implant's fetches /$/boot and XOR-decrypts a response. Check whether the parent node was importing @joyfill and whether the python child touched browser/keychain paths. 2) Contain: kill the node→child process tree, isolate the host, and rotate credentials if the python stager ran. 3) Hunt: pull the child's network connections (UC2), and check %USERPROFILE%\.npm or /tmp/.npm for a staged encrypted archive; scope other hosts running node-gyp vs. the implant by parent bundle path.

| order by Timestamp desc

Developer-tool binaries patched by node/python (Joyfill self-reload persistence) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Joyfill implant's persistence: node or python modifying trusted developer-tool files that run routinely — the @vscode/deviceid module (VS Code/Cursor/Antigravity), Discord desktop core, GitHub Desktop main.js, and the global npm CLI — to inject a self-reloading block. Rationale: Anchored on the article's named persistence targets (@vscode/deviceid, Discord core, GitHub Desktop main.js, global npm CLI) combined with a node/python initiator — legitimate updates to these apps come from their own installers/updaters, not from node.exe or python, making the initiator a high-fidelity discriminator. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/hijacked-npm-vscode-tasks-blockchain/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/seven-malicious-vite-npm-packages-use.html
ATT&CKT1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • VS Code / Cursor writing @vscode/deviceid on first launch via its own node-based Electron runtime
  • npm self-update ('npm install -g npm') legitimately rewriting the global npm CLI files
  • Discord auto-updater refreshing core modules
  • GitHub Desktop updater rewriting main.js during a version bump
  • Developer manually editing a node_modules file for local debugging
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "install" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "npm" and FolderPath has "\\npm\\node_modules\\npm\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the modified file and grep for the injected self-reloading marker tags (C250617A/C250618A/C250619A/C250620A/C260511A/C260512A/RS260605) and the '9-0135-3' campaign marker; confirm the writing process was the malicious node/python tree, not the app's own updater. 2) Contain: isolate the host, restore the affected developer-tool files from a clean source (reinstall VS Code/Discord/GitHub Desktop, 'npm install -g npm@latest'), and remove the 2773 packages. 3) Hunt: because these files run on every app launch, treat the machine as persistently compromised — rotate all developer credentials, and sweep other hosts for the same marker tags in @vscode/deviceid.

| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileRenamed","FileCreated")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\@vscode\deviceid", @"\GitHub Desktop\", @"\Discord\", @"\npm\node_modules\npm\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","python.exe","pythonw.exe","python3.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where EventType in ("FileModified","FileCreated","FileRenamed")

| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","python")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("166.88.134.62", "23.27.13.43", "198.105.127.210", "23.27.202.27") or RemoteUrl has_any ("api.trongrid.io", "fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com", "bsc-dataseed.binance.org", "bsc-rpc.publicnode.com", "ip-api.com")

let BadIPs     = dynamic(["166.88.134.62", "23.27.13.43", "198.105.127.210", "23.27.202.27"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["api.trongrid.io", "fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com", "bsc-dataseed.binance.org", "bsc-rpc.publicnode.com", "ip-api.com"]);
ImNetworkSession

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows

        Image|endswith:

            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3") or SHA1 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3") or MD5 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3") or SHA1 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3") or MD5 in~ ("26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["26351aed0397158d3a3b8cc8fd3047d4c015d264c9895f10f20f1521b974ed18", "36ff00b45e67baa7e3674b0c80f48e88737264c61e5c6b3b091200972de8157c", "cb46f12d70824ea24ed1f8bcf45bf3f86680e02a9089aafc03b27f691be57be3"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] vBulletin CVE-2026-61511 pre-auth RCE via ajax/render/pagenav template request
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] vBulletin web-server process (php-fpm/apache/nginx) spawning OS shell after CVE-2026-61511
vBulletin CVE-2026-61511 pre-auth RCE via ajax/render/pagenav template request AIExploitation High
Hunts direct HTTP requests to the vBulletin 'ajax/render/pagenav' render endpoint carrying a malformed 'pagenav[pagenumber]' value — the exact route/parameter Egidio Romano's PoC abuses to reach runMaths()->eval(). Legitimate clients never POST this template route directly, so a crafted hit is a high-fidelity exploitation attempt against an unpatched (<=5.7.5 / <=6.2.1) instance. Rationale: Uses the exact PoC route 'ajax/render/pagenav' and the 'pagenav[pagenumber]' parameter named in the SSD advisory and article, plus a phpfuck-style special-char burst (^()!~) that the regex-bypass payload requires. Direct external requests to this internal render template are not legitimate user traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://ssd-disclosure.com/vbulletin-runtime-template-runmaths-preauth-rce/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/public-exploit-released-for-patched.html • https://securityonline.info/vbulletin-preauth-rce-cve-2026-61511/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/vbulletin-flaw-execute-php-code/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Acunetix) probing the CVE-2026-61511 endpoint
  • Internal red-team / pentest validating the patch level
  • Security researchers or bug-bounty testers hitting a staging forum
  • WAF-in-monitor-mode replaying blocked payloads into access logs
  • Uptime/synthetic monitors misconfigured to request raw ajax/render paths
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestClientApplication has_any ("Nessus", "Qualys", "Acunetix", "masscan", "zgrab") or DeviceAction in ("blocked", "denied", "deny"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the target host's vBulletin version (banner / footer / admincp) is <=5.7.5 or <=6.2.1 and check the HTTP status returned — a 200 to a POSTed pagenav render with a non-numeric pagenumber implies successful reach into runMaths(). Pull the full request body from the WAF/proxy. 2) Contain: Block the source IP at the WAF, virtual-patch the ajax/render/pagenav route, and expedite upgrade to 6.2.2 or Patch Level 1 (6.2.1/6.2.0/6.1.6); 5.x has no fix so isolate/decommission. 3) Hunt: Pivot to UC2 on the web host for php-fpm/apache spawning shells within seconds of the request, and review outbound connections from the web-server account for reverse shells or tool download.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "ajax/render/pagenav"
| where RequestMethod == "POST" or RequestURL has "pagenav[pagenumber]" or RequestURL matches regex @"[\^\(\)!~]{4,}"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

vBulletin web-server process (php-fpm/apache/nginx) spawning OS shell after CVE-2026-61511 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the post-exploitation stage of CVE-2026-61511: the vBulletin PHP runtime executing arbitrary system() commands via eval(), which surfaces as php-fpm/php/httpd/apache2/nginx spawning a shell or recon/download binary under the web-server account. This is the RCE actually landing, independent of whether the exploit request was logged. Rationale: Chains directly off the article's mechanism: runMaths() feeds attacker input to PHP eval(), and the public PoC calls system() for an interactive shell under the web-server account — so php-fpm/apache/nginx as parent of sh/curl/whoami is the RCE landing. Parent-child pairing (not bare shell) keeps fidelity high. Cross-checked against: • https://ssd-disclosure.com/vbulletin-runtime-template-runmaths-preauth-rce/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/public-exploit-released-for-patched.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/vbulletin-flaw-execute-php-code/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • vBulletin/CI cron jobs where PHP legitimately shells out (image processing via ImageMagick 'convert', 'sendmail' mail delivery)
  • Backup/maintenance scripts run under www-data invoking tar/curl
  • Plugin functionality that calls exec() for thumbnails or media transcoding (ffmpeg)
  • Composer/deploy automation running as the web user
  • Monitoring agents launched under the web-server service account
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ImageMagick", "convert ", "ffmpeg", "sendmail", "/usr/sbin/") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "cron")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — phpfuck RCE typically yields short recon (id/whoami/uname) or a download (curl/wget to an external IP). Correlate the process time with a UC1 ajax/render/pagenav request from the same host within ~60s. 2) Contain: Isolate the web host, kill the offending php-fpm worker and child, rotate any DB/API creds readable by the web account, and block observed egress IPs. 3) Hunt: Search for dropped webshells under the vBulletin docroot (FileWritten of .php by the web user), new cron entries/service units for persistence, and lateral SSH/DB auth from the compromised host.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

Poweradmin OIDC/SAML/logout endpoint hit with anomalous Host header (CVE-2026-54588) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to Poweradmin's OIDC, SAML and logout authentication endpoints where the Host header resolves to a hostname never before seen on those paths. CVE-2026-54588 lets an unauthenticated attacker poison HTTP_HOST so the redirect_uri/ACS/SLO URL sent to the IdP points at attacker infrastructure, so a novel Host on /oidc/, /saml/ or /logout is the exploitation primitive itself. Rationale: Uses the article-specific endpoints (/oidc/, /saml/, /logout) that build callback URLs from HTTP_HOST, and flags the Host header value that is the exploitation payload. attacker.com in the PoC is illustrative only, so the detection keys on Host-header novelty rather than a hardcoded domain. Defender AH has no inbound-web-request table, hence defender_kql/falcon/cloudwatch left empty. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-54588 • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-54588/ • https://github.com/poweradmin/poweradmin/security/advisories/GHSA-3735-5339-xfwx
ATT&CKT1190 T1528
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A new legitimate FQDN/vhost added to the load balancer during a migration or cutover appears as a novel Host on the auth paths
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/nuclei) deliberately sending crafted Host headers to test for host-header injection
  • Health-check probes or CDN edge nodes issuing requests with an IP-literal or internal Host value
  • Multi-tenant reverse proxy fronting Poweradmin under several legitimate customer FQDNs the 30-day baseline hasn't warmed up on
Suppression filter
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","nuclei","masscan","zgrab","Expanse")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the flagged HttpHostName + SrcIpAddr; confirm the host is NOT a legitimate Poweradmin FQDN or internal health-check target. Check the same source IP for follow-on /oidc/callback requests carrying a code parameter. 2) Contain: set interface.base_url in config/settings.php to the canonical URL (activates the safe branch) and upgrade Poweradmin to 4.2.4/4.3.3; at the proxy, hard-pin the Host header instead of proxy_set_header Host $http_host. 3) Hunt: review PowerDNS/Poweradmin admin audit for zone edits (MX, SPF/DKIM TXT, CAA removal, NS delegation) originating from sessions after the anomalous host, and force-logout/rotate sessions for any admin who authenticated in that window.
let LookbackHours = 24h;
let AuthPaths = dynamic(["/oidc/","/saml/","/logout"]);
let Baseline = ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(LookbackHours))
| where Url has_any (AuthPaths)
| where isnotempty(HttpHostName)
| summarize by HttpHostName;

| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
| where Url has_any (AuthPaths)
| where isnotempty(HttpHostName)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on HttpHostName
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Requests=count(), SampleUrl=any(Url), UserAgents=make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent,10) by HttpHostName, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname
| order by FirstSeen desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eventstats dc(src) as distinctSrc by site
| sort - firstTime

| tstats summariesonly=false count as requests min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where (Web.url="*/oidc/*" OR Web.url="*/saml/*" OR Web.url="*/logout*") by Web.site, Web.dest, Web.src, Web.uri_path, Web.http_user_agent

Entra ID AADSTS50011 redirect_uri mismatch burst (Poweradmin OIDC host poisoning) AIExploitation Medium
Alerts on Entra ID sign-in failures with result code 50011 (redirect URI does not match the app registration). When CVE-2026-54588 poisons Poweradmin's redirect_uri to an attacker host, Entra rejects the poisoned reply URL with AADSTS50011 — so a sudden appearance of 50011 for a normally-working OIDC app is a direct signature of the injection attempt. Rationale: Cross-checked that AADSTS50011 is Entra's redirect-URI-mismatch code surfaced as ResultType/ErrorCode 50011 in sign-in logs; a poisoned redirect_uri from the CVE is exactly what triggers it, giving a clean deployable alert without needing to know the attacker domain. Falcon/CloudWatch left empty as this is Entra sign-in telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/entra/entra-id/app-integration/error-code-aadsts50011-redirect-uri-mismatch • https://github.com/poweradmin/poweradmin/security/advisories/GHSA-3735-5339-xfwx
ATT&CKT1528 T1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate redirect-URI misconfiguration right after a Poweradmin upgrade or interface.base_url change
  • App registration reply URL edited by an admin but not yet propagated (3-5 minute window) producing transient 50011s
  • Scheme mismatch (http vs https) behind a TLS-terminating proxy that isn't forwarding X-Forwarded-Proto
  • Developer/test tenant experimenting with a new redirect URI in non-production
Suppression filter
| where SourceIPs !has "AWS Internal" | where AppDisplayName !has "test" and AppDisplayName !has "dev"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the AppDisplayName/AppId is the Poweradmin OIDC app and that it authenticated cleanly before this burst; inspect ResultDescription for the rejected redirect URI and note its host — a foreign host = confirmed poisoning. 2) Contain: temporarily disable the Poweradmin app registration or tighten Conditional Access, set interface.base_url and patch to 4.2.4/4.3.3, and pin Host at the reverse proxy. 3) Hunt: check whether any 50011 attempts were followed by a successful sign-in (attacker completing the flow to a registered URI), review the source IPs against the UC1 web-log hits, and audit PowerDNS zone changes (MX/SPF/DKIM/CAA) for the affected admins.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 50011
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Attempts=count(), Users=dcount(AccountUpn), SourceIPs=make_set(IPAddress,25) by Application, ApplicationId, ResourceDisplayName
| order by Attempts desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == "50011"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Attempts=count(), Users=dcount(UserPrincipalName), SourceIPs=make_set(IPAddress,25) by AppDisplayName, AppId, ResultDescription
| order by Attempts desc

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,

// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),

         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Tengu Botnet Reboots Compromised Linux Devices When Defenders Kill Its Process

The Hacker News
2026-07-28 11 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A new Mirai-derived botnet called Tengu can use a compromised Linux device's hardware watchdog to trigger a reboot when defenders kill its main process. If that happens, Tengu's other persistence mechanisms get another chance to relaunch it. Nozomi Networks Labs observed the dropper reaching its honeypots through Telnet credential brute force. Tengu supports 25 distributed denial-of-service (

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Telnet credential brute force against internet-exposed IoT/Linux devices (Tengu dropper entry) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Tengu ELF-header corruption ('ELFOOD') of Linux reboot/shutdown utilities · [LLM] Tengu guardian process masquerading as kernel thread [kworker/0:0] · [LLM] Tengu immutable-binary persistence via chattr +i on Linux/IoT
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Tengu botnet C2 / IPFS beacon to 64.89.163.8 on TCP 9931 and 8080 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Telnet credential brute force against internet-exposed IoT/Linux devices (Tengu dropper entry) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts high-volume inbound Telnet (TCP/23) connection attempts from a single external source against Linux/IoT hosts, the entry vector Nozomi observed for the Tengu dropper on its honeypots. Article-specific because Tengu spreads exclusively via Telnet default/weak-credential brute force rather than an exploit. Rationale: Uses the article's stated entry vector (Telnet TCP/23 credential brute force on internet-exposed IoT/Linux) as a volumetric single-source pivot; port 23 to public-facing embedded hosts is inherently high-signal since legitimate Telnet exposure is rare. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tengu-botnet-reboots-compromised-linux.html
ATT&CKT1110 T1078.001 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal network/security scanner (Shodan-style, Nessus, Nmap) sweeping TCP/23 across the estate
  • A misconfigured legacy management tool that legitimately polls Telnet on embedded gear
  • ISP/upstream background internet scanning noise hitting an exposed device
  • Load-balancer or NAT health checks probing port 23
  • Penetration-test engagement against IoT segment
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<known_scanner_ips>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target hosts are IoT/embedded and that TCP/23 is genuinely internet-reachable; check whether any attempt succeeded (post-auth session, new process). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the perimeter, disable/firewall Telnet on the exposed devices, and rotate any default credentials. 3) Hunt: on any device that accepted a session, pivot to Tengu post-compromise indicators — outbound TCP/9931 to 64.89.163.8, a process masquerading as [kworker/0:0], chattr +i on new binaries, and modified /sbin/reboot|shutdown utilities.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where LocalPort == 23 and RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Attempts = count(), Devices = dcount(DeviceId), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by RemoteIP
| where Attempts > 20   // empirical Telnet brute-force volume threshold from a single source
| order by Attempts desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DestinationPort == 23
| summarize Attempts = count(), Denied = countif(DeviceAction in~ ("deny","drop","blocked","reset")), Targets = dcount(DestinationIP), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP
| where Attempts > 20   // brute-force volume threshold on Telnet/23 from a single source
| order by Attempts desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as attempts, dc(All_Traffic.dest) as targets, min(_time) as firstSeen, max(_time) as lastSeen from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=23 All_Traffic.transport=tcp by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.action | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where attempts>20 | sort - attempts
| tstats summariesonly=false count as attempts, dc(All_Traffic.dest) as targets, min(_time) as firstSeen, max(_time) as lastSeen from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_port=23 All_Traffic.transport=tcp by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.action | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where attempts>20 | sort - attempts
Tengu botnet C2 / IPFS beacon to 64.89.163.8 on TCP 9931 and 8080 AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any egress from an internal host to the hardcoded Tengu C2 IP 64.89.163.8 over TCP/9931 (plaintext registration/heartbeat) or TCP/8080 (IPFS gateway payload retrieval). Article-specific because both the IP and the two ports are named in the analyzed sample's configuration. Rationale: The C2 IP 64.89.163.8 and both ports (9931 for plaintext registration/heartbeat, 8080 for the IPFS gateway) are explicit strings from the analyzed sample; a hardcoded single-IP + non-standard-port pair is near-zero-FP. URLhaus independently logged 17 malicious Mirai-related URLs at the same IP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/tengu-botnet-reboots-compromised-linux.html • https://urlhaus.abuse.ch/host/64.89.163.8/
ATT&CKT1571 T1071.001 T1105 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate IPFS node/user on the estate happening to reach port 8080 on that host (unlikely — IP is a known-bad C2)
  • Threat-intel or sandbox detonation VM deliberately beaconing to the IOC during analysis
  • Security researcher/blue-team validating the IOC from a lab host
  • Stale NAT/proxy log attributing the connection to the wrong internal source
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal source device and the initiating process (Defender InitiatingProcessFileName / Falcon ContextImageFileName); confirm the host is IoT/Linux. 2) Contain: block 64.89.163.8 at the perimeter, isolate the device from the network, and preserve volatile state before power actions (Tengu corrupts reboot/shutdown binaries). 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts beaconing to the same IP/ports, and on the infected host review systemd units, /etc/init.d, /etc/rc.local, shell rc files, cron, and /dev/watchdog before reimaging.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "64.89.163.8"
| where RemotePort in (9931, 8080)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "64.89.163.8"
| where DestinationPort in (9931, 8080)
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHost = SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceAction, ApplicationProtocol, RequestURL
| order by TimeGenerated desc
